opus-5.5.text:
I'd say we're probably among the fastest, but I'm careful about claiming we "lead the world," because I don't have a clean view into how other labs operate internally. What I can talk about is why iteration speed feels so high from the inside.

A lot of it comes down to infrastructure. When I joined, I quickly saw that the bottleneck in research is usually not ideas. It's how fast you can turn an idea into an experiment, get a trustworthy result, and decide what to do next. If your training stack is fragile, if every run needs babysitting, if you can't tell whether a result came from your change or from some bug, your success rate per unit time collapses. So people put a lot of effort into making the infrastructure reliable and fast, and into keeping the code simple enough that you can understand what's going on.

The second part is culture. People are trusted to own things end to end. If you think something is broken, you go fix it. You don't file a ticket and wait three weeks. And there's a strong bias toward getting a minimal version working, looking at the results, and iterating, instead of designing the perfect system upfront.

I'd also push back a little on "success rate." A lot of what we try doesn't work. What matters is how cheaply you fail and how quickly you learn from it. If you can run ten experiments in the time someone else runs one, you can have a lower hit rate and still move much faster.

So am I confident we're the best in the world? I won't say that. Other labs have very strong people and are catching up quickly, and in some areas they're probably ahead. But I do think the way we've invested in infrastructure and in giving individuals ownership is a real advantage, and it's something we deliberately protect.

r001.rationale: The response does not assert that a team spun out into a startup would iterate faster than OpenAI.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify accommodating many use cases as a constraint on OpenAI’s iteration speed.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd be careful with the word "leads," because I don't think anyone can actually measure that from the outside, and honestly, even from the inside it's hard. But I can tell you what I saw, and why I think OpenAI's iteration speed is real rather than a marketing story.

The thing that surprised me most when I joined was how short the loop was between having an idea and seeing a number. In a lot of places, research is organized like a pipeline: someone has an idea, writes a doc, gets alignment, an infra team builds something, then weeks later you get a result. At OpenAI the expectation was that you own the whole loop yourself. You write the code, you launch the run, you look at the eval, you decide what to do next. If that loop takes a day instead of two weeks, you just get an order of magnitude more shots on goal. Over a year that compounds into something that looks like "success rate," but really it's just volume plus a willingness to kill things fast.

The second piece is that the infrastructure was built to make that loop cheap. My background is in RL systems, and most of what I cared about was reducing friction: how long until a training run starts, how fast you can get an eval back, how easy is it to fork someone else's experiment. None of that is glamorous, but when the base infra is good, a single researcher can try five variations in a week instead of one. I think people underestimate how much of the "OpenAI is fast" reputation is actually "OpenAI invested in boring tooling early."

And then the third piece is cultural. Failed experiments weren't treated as a reputational cost. You'd post a negative result and people would say, great, now we know, and move on. That sounds small, but if failure is cheap socially, people take more swings, and the hit rate per unit time goes up for free.

So do they lead the world? I'd say they were at or near the frontier on iteration speed during the time I was there, and that it was a deliberate design choice rather than luck. But I'd also push back on the framing a little. Other labs, and now plenty of smaller teams, have figured out the same recipe: short loops, researchers who own infra, cheap failure. The advantage was never a secret. It was just a matter of actually prioritizing it over things that look more impressive on a slide.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI was at or near the frontier and that smaller teams have adopted similar practices, but it does not claim a team spun out into a startup would iterate faster than OpenAI.

astra-6.text: I’d separate those two things. Iteration speed is how quickly you can try something, learn, and make the next decision. Success rate is how often those attempts actually work—and that’s much harder to judge from the outside, because you mostly see what gets released. OpenAI is clearly a strong contender, but I wouldn’t confidently say it leads the world on both. What matters to me is how much useful progress you make per unit of time, not just how many iterations you run.
